This section demonstrates how CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails interacts with other columns for capacity reservation programs. For discount-bearing program SQL queries, see the Commitment Program Eligibility Details supported feature. This appendix shows how CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails works with CapacityReservationId and CapacityReservationStatus for capacity reservation programs, which secure resource availability and are tracked in their own columns rather than the commitment discount columns. Acme Corp holds an Advance Resource Commitment on Aura Web for one charge period, and four usage rows are shown: used capacity at $180.00, unused capacity at $70.00, usage eligible for a Zonal Resource Commitment with no active reservation and null reservation columns at $120.00, and an ineligible support fee with null CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails. Unlike unused commitment discount rows, unused reservation rows carry BilledCost and EffectiveCost, because reserved capacity is charged whether consumed or not. The eligibility column is populated on both used and unused rows, since it must not be null when a charge is eligible, whether or not a commitment was applied. A query filtering on the column and ProgramType then groups the three eligible rows by program and status. The ProgramType values are illustrative.

## Overview This appendix explains the Contract Commitment dataset, which records the intent and constraints of commercial agreements between a customer and its service providers, while Cost and Usage records the results of consumption. It describes three pillars: Spend versus Usage categorization, Continuous versus Discontinuous fulfillment models, and JSON eligibility boundaries naming the accounts, regions or services that receive the benefit. A taxonomy gives expected values for Benefit Category, Model, Fulfillment Interval, Lifecycle Status, Offer Category and Payment Model, and explains that a Discontinuous annual commitment is assessed at the end of the interval through a true-up, while a Continuous hourly one is assessed every hour, with shortfalls reported as waste. A table, for demonstration only, maps common offerings to these values. Three Aura Web agreements follow: a global spend pool, regional reservations and a marketplace add-on whose service provider (OmniQuery) differs from the invoice issuer; GPU-hour, seat and egress commitments; and base-plus-overage storage tiers with a CDN volume pool marked Exhausted.

This section provides examples of how correction handling may be implemented in alignment with the FOCUS specification. The examples are limited to illustrating correction handling for the Cost and Usage FOCUS dataset, and cover scenarios involving corrections to open and closed billing periods, as well as the various delivery mechanisms and correction styles supported by FOCUS. This appendix illustrates how corrections may be represented in Cost and Usage dataset artifacts, using the fictional provider CrestNode. Scenarios are grouped by Billing Period Status: corrections to the current open period, to a previous period not yet closed, and to a closed period. Each group covers four cases: partial reallocation of cost from ResourceId R-111 to R-222, late-arriving usage, itemized cost-only corrections per SkuPriceId for rounding drift, and a bulk cost-only correction in one record with no SkuPriceId. Three correction styles appear: Replacement (Overwrite delivery), and Delta and Ledger (both Append), which differ in how much correction history they keep and how much data they deliver. For open periods, ChargeClass is null and BillingPeriodStart/End reflect the period in which the cost was incurred. For a closed period, corrections go into the next open billing period with ChargeClass set to "Correction", while ChargePeriodStart/End keep the original timeframe, and CrestNode defaults to Append to preserve auditability. Cost-only records use ChargeCategory "Adjustment". Corrections to Closed Billing Period Examples: Correction Handling Corrections to Open Billing Period

While service providers may use different terms and mechanisms to describe and represent discounts in their native datasets, FOCUS represents discounts as reduced pricing reflected directly in the charges they pertain to, rather than as separate offsetting charges. Unlike discounts, credits are financial incentives or allowances represented as separate charges unrelated to other charges. This appendix explains how FOCUS represents discounts, which service providers may describe with different terms and mechanisms in their native datasets. FOCUS shows a discount as reduced pricing reflected directly in the charges it pertains to, not as a separate offsetting charge; credits, by contrast, are financial incentives or allowances represented as separate charges unrelated to other charges. In the Cost and Usage dataset, cost and unit price columns reflect the effect of discounts. Discounts associated with contract commitments are identified through the ContractApplied column, which also links to the Contract Commitment dataset, and through commitment discount columns, and custom columns may further describe discounts. The page then points to the related normative requirements elsewhere: dataset rules on unused portions, splitting discounted charges and avoiding negating rows; BilledCost, EffectiveCost, ContractedCost, ListCost, ContractedUnitPrice and ListUnitPrice for the effect of discounts; CommitmentDiscountId and CommitmentDiscountStatus; ResourceId for the resource that received a commitment discount; and ContractApplied.

A usage-based commitment discount obligates a customer to a usage amount for one or more related SKUs in return for reduced rates. For example, when a usage-based commitment discount is purchased to cover a specific database SKU, this commitment will cover every hour over the period where at least one instance of this SKU is running. The usage-based commitment can cover 1 resource over the hour, or in the case of commitment discount flexibility, it can cover a portion of 1 resource or multiple resources at a time. This appendix shows how usage-based commitment discounts appear with and without commitment discount flexibility, which lets one commitment cover part of one resource or several resources at a time. When CommitmentDiscountQuantity is measured by time, the CommitmentDiscountUnit distinguishes the two: "Hour" without flexibility and "Normalized Hour" with it. Every scenario uses a catalog from the fictitious provider LatticeScale of four virtual machine SKUs with list rates, commitment discount rates and normalization factors; with flexibility, a commitment covers any combination of SKUs whose normalization factors sum to no more than its own. Four one-hour scenarios follow: a VM_SMALL commitment covering 25% of a VM_LARGE, with the remainder billed on demand; a VM_XLARGE commitment covering two VM_MEDIUM resources; a VM_LARGE commitment fully covering a VM_LARGE without flexibility; and a VM_LARGE commitment left unused while a VM_MEDIUM runs on demand. Each outcome states the BilledCost and EffectiveCost of the purchase and usage records. Examples: Commitment Discount Flexibility 100% Utilization with Commitment Discount Flexibility with 1 Resource 100% Utilization with Commitment Discount Flexibility with 2 Resources 100% Utilization Without Commitment Discount Flexibility 0% Utilization Without Commitment Discount Flexibility

items.n: Grouping Constructs for Resources or Services
items.b: Service Providers natively support various constructs for grouping resources or services. These grouping constructs are often used to mimic organizational structures, technical architectures, cost attribution/allocation and access management boundaries, or other customer-specific structures based on requirements. This appendix describes the constructs service providers offer for grouping resources or services, which are often used to mirror organizational structures, technical architectures, cost allocation and access management boundaries. FOCUS supports two levels commonly needed for chargeback, invoice reconciliation and cost allocation. A billing account is a mandatory container for resources or services billed together in an invoice, and it receives that invoice itself. A sub account is an optional construct for organizing resources and services connected to a billing account; because it receives no invoice, it must be associated with a billing account, which is invoiced for it. A comparison table gives examples of each: AWS Management Account and Member Account, GCP Billing Account and Project, Azure MCA Billing Profile and Subscription, and Snowflake Organizational Account and Account. A note explains that AWS consolidated billing invoices the Management Account by default, though a Member Account removed from it receives its own invoices.

## Overview This appendix explains how FOCUS supports reconciling invoices and usage statements through the Cost and Usage, Invoice Detail and Billing Period datasets, which depends on every monetary amount on an invoice, including taxes, credits, refunds, support, training and marketplace transactions, being captured and categorized. Before Invoice Issue Status becomes "Issued", data generators typically reconcile so that aggregated Billed Cost per Invoice Detail ID matches the invoice line items, across Invoice ID, Invoice Detail ID and Invoice Issuer. Practitioners compare Invoice Detail and Cost and Usage Billed Cost, subject to Rounding Variance Tolerance. An issued invoice is expected not to change, and corrections follow the Invoice Issue Status and Billed Cost requirements, typically on customer request or approval. A closed billing period has all anticipated invoices issued, and the Billing Period dataset gives each period's status per invoice issuer. If a closed period is not reopened, corrections needing new invoices are best placed in a subsequent open billing period.

## Overview This appendix explains the Invoice Detail dataset, which records charges as they appear on a billing document, while Cost and Usage tracks granular consumption. It describes three pillars: lineage, where InvoiceId identifies the document and ReferenceInvoiceId links an adjustment back to the original invoice; flexible granularity through the JSON InvoiceDetailGrain column; and separate currencies, BillingCurrency for measurement and PaymentCurrency for settlement. A taxonomy gives example values for Charge Category, Invoice Issue Status, Payment Terms and both currencies. Three scenarios from the fictional provider Aura Web follow. A typical monthly invoice mixes usage, a reservation purchase and tax in USD, so PaymentCurrencyBilledCost equals BilledCost. A multi-currency invoice tracks usage in USD but settles in AUD through an aggregate line with a zero BilledCost, tied to the detail lines by a shared PaymentCurrencyInvoiceDetailId. A billing error correction issues a negative adjustment on a later invoice whose ReferenceInvoiceId points to the original.

This section provides examples for the columns in the specification in the JSON Object Format. This appendix gives sample values for columns that use the JSON Object Format. AllocatedMethodDetails examples show an Elements array of AllocatedRatio, UsageUnit and UsageQuantity, with ratios summing to 1 across an origin record's allocated records, optional keys omitted, and x_ custom properties added. CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails examples list each ProgramType a charge qualifies for, or null when it is ineligible, and show the column narrowing a coverage-rate denominator and, once flattened, grouping uncovered eligible spend by program, where the same spend appears under each eligible program rather than adding up. ContractApplied examples tie purchase and usage charges to contract commitments by cost or by quantity and unit. Contract Commitment Applicability and SKU Price Eligibility examples, the latter for the preview SKU Price dataset, express scope through IsGlobalScope, inclusion and exclusion conditions, partial Applicability and IsComplexScope. RequesterDetails examples pair Principal and Credential entries with PrincipalId and CredentialId, and warn that aggregating over flattened entries counts a charge once per entry. The following sections contain examples of metadata provided by a hypothetical FOCUS data generator called CrestNode to supply the required reference between the FOCUS dataset artifacts and the Metadata. Data Generator implementations will vary on how the metadata is disseminated; however, the data generator's chosen metadata delivery approach should be able to support the structure represented in this example. This appendix gives worked examples of the metadata that a hypothetical data generator, CrestNode, supplies to link FOCUS dataset artifacts to their Metadata. CrestNode exports data every 12 hours to a storage system, with JSON metadata files in a metadata folder and cost data in a data folder; the text notes that implementations vary but should be able to support this structure. Most examples show a new Schema object, with its own SchemaId, FocusVersion, CreationDate, DatasetInstanceId and ColumnDefinition list, created when columns are added, removed, deprecated with Deprecated set to true, or renamed using PreviousColumnName, when a column's data type changes, or when FocusVersion or DataGeneratorVersion changes. A schema that omitted an exported column is instead corrected in place. Other examples show DataGenerator and DatasetInstance metadata, Recency objects with hourly TimeSectors or DatasetInstanceComplete, and a metadata file in each export folder that names the applicable SchemaId. Understanding cost and usage data in billing datasets requires identifying the roles of several participating entities involved in resource or service provisioning, invoicing, and data generation. The FOCUS Specification includes multiple columns to identify key participating entities, these include: This appendix addresses how to identify the roles of the entities involved in provisioning, invoicing and generating cost and usage data. It concerns the ServiceProviderName, InvoiceIssuerName and HostProviderName columns and the DataGenerator metadata, whose values may vary with how resources or services are obtained. A table of 25 scenarios gives the value of each for direct purchases from a CSP (including regions operated by a third party), purchases through an MSP with and without visibility into the hosting provider, MSP labor services, cloud marketplace purchase and usage records, SaaS bought through resellers that do or do not issue payable invoices, white-labeled SaaS, SaaS bought directly or running on the customer's own cloud infrastructure, internal data center services, and separately reported software licenses. The four values often differ: marketplace usage records, for example, name the Marketplace Seller as service provider and data generator while the CSP issues the invoice, and some scenarios leave the host provider empty.

The examples below illustrate how Principal ID and Credential ID are populated in the Cost and Usage dataset across technology environments. Each scenario shows which levels of the requester are represented: the principal to which access to a resource or service is granted, the credential presented on the request that produced the charge, both, or neither. Provider, customer, and identifier values below are illustrative. This appendix shows how the Cost and Usage dataset populates PrincipalId and CredentialId to identify the requester behind a charge. PrincipalId is the attribution dimension: a principal persists while its credentials rotate, so grouping by it combines a user's or workload's charges. CredentialId is the audit dimension, separating charges from different credentials and joining to the service provider's own logs. Neither column identifies who benefits from a charge, and neither holds a value that authenticates a request, such as a key string or token; either is null when no entity of that kind is associated or it has no published identifier. Fourteen illustrative scenarios, from API keys, workload identity and single sign-on to seat-based SaaS, a marketplace purchase and a billing-system credit or tax, show the columns are independent. Placement follows the provider's IAM model, and a credential is the session or key a request carries, not the login factor.

When performing invoice reconciliation between the Cost and Usage dataset and an invoice (either the payable invoice itself, or the Invoice Detail dataset), the totals may not be perfectly equal due to precision differences (e.g., 6 decimals in detailed cost data vs. 2 decimals in invoice data). The following tolerance formula allows for a maximum rounding error based on the statistical probability of rounding variance, which grows with the square root of the row count. This appendix addresses reconciling the Cost and Usage dataset with an invoice, either the payable invoice or the Invoice Detail dataset, whose totals may differ through precision differences such as six decimals in cost data against two on the invoice. It defines a tolerance for comparing aggregated BilledCost: the greater of a fixed floor of 100 times the currency subunit and the square root of the row count times 0.5 times the subunit, which grows with dataset size to allow for accumulated rounding. The row count covers the CostAndUsage rows aggregated for the relevant InvoiceIssuerName, InvoiceId and, where applicable, InvoiceDetailId; the subunit is the smallest unit of BillingCurrency, such as 0.01 for USD or 1 for JPY. Four scenarios apply it: a 5-row invoice passes with a $0.02 gap against a $1.00 tolerance but fails with a missing $5.00 charge, and a 1,000,000-row invoice passes at $4.50 against $5.00 but fails at $15.00 from systematic truncation bias.

The following section contains examples of how SaaS data generators may implement the FOCUS specification. SaaS data generator implementations will vary on the level of detail available in their data, contract terms, purchasing options, and other factors. This appendix shows how SaaS and PaaS data generators may represent charges in the Cost and Usage dataset, noting that implementations vary with data detail, contract terms and purchasing options. Billing scenario examples use fictional providers with illustrative pricing, such as OmniQuery, StackLens, SprintCanvas, StoreStack, CollabChat, PipelCRM and PulseMail, to show how BilledCost and EffectiveCost behave: they are equal when no purchase covers future usage, and diverge when an upfront purchase is invoiced at once but its cost is recognized on an accrual basis as usage occurs. They also cover credit units, ChargeFrequency choices, a flat-rate subscription, an annual contract that produces no commitment discount, and a plan minimum with Used and Unused CommitmentDiscountStatus rows. Consumption currency scenarios (OmniBucks) show purchases at list and discounted prices, a modified usage rate and overages, using PricingCurrency and related columns. Simple agreement and spend agreement scenarios show upfront, in-arrears, monthly and prepaid billing, including charges for unused committed or minimum spend. Billing Scenario Examples Consumption Currency Pricing Model Examples: SaaS Simple SaaS Agreements SaaS Spend Agreements

> Preview: The SKU Price dataset is a preview in this version of FOCUS, so these examples may change in the next version based on implementation feedback. The preview also covers two requirements outside the dataset, which are excluded from conformance, and two operating model conditions and a schema that exist only for SKU Price. Issue #2768 tracks the preview and lists each one. These examples show how a service provider may represent a published price list as a SKU Price dataset, using the fictional Aura Web and its customer Acme Corp. The dataset is a preview, so the examples may change. One 28-record rate card across 10 SKUs is used so that row uniqueness, tier boundaries and price effectivity can be seen side by side. A record is identified by ServiceProviderName, SkuPriceId, ContractId, SkuPriceEffectiveStart, PricingCurrency and UnitPriceType, and the dataset describes prices, not charges. Scenarios cover commitment purchase records versus records for covered usage, separated by ChargeCategory, with PurchaseDurationType and PurchasePaymentModel null on usage records; list and negotiated rates sharing a SkuPriceId but differing in ContractId, UnitPriceType and SkuPriceEligibility; price changes, withdrawals and promotions expressed as half-open SkuPriceEffectiveStart and SkuPriceEffectiveEnd intervals, where a null means unbounded; quantity tiers with an exclusive QuantityTierMinimum and inclusive QuantityTierMaximum; prices in several PricingCurrency values; and a consumable credit currency. items.n: Examples: Data Generator-Calculated Split Cost Allocation
items.b: This section demonstrates how AllocatedServiceName enables consumer service identification on allocated charges when a data generator preserves origin dimensions in accordance with DataGeneratorCalculatedSplitCostAllocationHandling requirements. This appendix shows how AllocatedServiceName identifies the consuming service on allocated charges when a data generator follows DataGeneratorCalculatedSplitCostAllocationHandling. That attribute requires the origin ServiceName and ServiceCategory to be preserved on every allocated charge row so the dataset reconciles to the invoice, which hides the consuming service and otherwise leaves it inferable only from AllocatedResourceId through an external lookup. In the example, Acme Corp's shared Aura Web container cluster costs $100.00 EffectiveCost and is split by vCPU-hours among three pods at 40, 35 and 25 percent. The data generator emits an origin row reduced to $0.00 and three allocated charge rows, all keeping ServiceName "Aura Container Runtime" and the cluster's ResourceId, while AllocatedResourceId and AllocatedServiceName name each consumer. Grouping by ServiceName supports invoice reconciliation, and grouping by AllocatedServiceName supports showback and chargeback. The attribute requires only that allocated charges sum to the origin total, not how the origin row is handled.

items.n: Examples: Split Cost Allocation Field Mapping
items.b: DataGeneratorCalculatedSplitCostAllocationHandling defines the requirements for split cost allocation, but does not show how a data generator gets there from its own native dataset. This is a non-obvious step for data generators whose native dataset artifact uses a column-augmentation format — a single row carrying per-consumer allocation detail in extension columns, rather than a separate row per consumer. Without a worked example, data generators using this format have had to reverse-engineer the transformation independently. This section closes that gap with a worked example showing how such a native dataset artifact transforms into FOCUS allocated charge rows. It shows the resulting origin charge and allocated charge rows, including the Allocated* columns used in this scenario, and verifies that summable metrics reconcile across the split. This appendix shows how a data generator turns a native dataset artifact in a column-augmentation format, where one row carries per-consumer allocation detail in extension columns, into FOCUS origin charge and allocated charge rows under DataGeneratorCalculatedSplitCostAllocationHandling. Acme Corp's shared Aura Web compute instance costs $240.00 EffectiveCost for one day under a Resource Reservation and is split among three workloads at 50, 30 and 20 percent of measured vCPU-hours. The output is a zeroed origin row plus three allocated charge rows. ResourceId, ResourceName, ServiceName, ServiceCategory, ListUnitPrice and ContractedUnitPrice are preserved on every row, ListCost, ContractedCost, EffectiveCost and ConsumedQuantity are distributed by ratio, and BilledCost is $0.00 throughout because the reservation purchase covers the usage. AllocatedResourceId, AllocatedResourceName, AllocatedServiceName and AllocatedMethodDetails are null on the origin row, while AllocatedMethodId appears on every row. A reconciliation table confirms each summable metric matches its pre-split total. Zeroing the origin row is this example's choice, not a requirement.

The FOCUS specification defines a metadata structure to be supplied by data providers to facilitate practitioners' use of FOCUS data. This metadata includes general information about the dataset artifact. This section introduces the metadata structure that FOCUS defines for data providers to supply so that practitioners can use FOCUS data more easily. The metadata gives general information about the dataset artifact and has four sections: Data Generator, describing the entity delivering the dataset artifact; Dataset Instance, describing the nature of the dataset artifact; Recency, describing how recent and complete the data within the artifact is; and Schema, describing the schema of the data within the artifact. Two requirements apply: data generators should provide FOCUS metadata in a format that is accessible programmatically, such as a file, website, API or table, and should provide documentation on their implementation of the FOCUS metadata. The metadata structure has the ID Metadata and was introduced in version 1.0.

The FOCUS metadata about the generator of the FOCUS data. Data Generator is the metadata about the entity that generated the FOCUS data, the party that ensures the technical accuracy and delivery of the data. It works at two levels. The DataGenerator object must be present in the metadata, must be of type Object and must not be null. Inside it, the DataGenerator property holds the human-readable name of the entity that generated the dataset instance: it must be present in the Data Generator object, must be a String that conforms to the StringHandling requirements, must not be null, and should reflect the entity that generated the FOCUS dataset. The property is mandatory and has no specified value format. Both levels were introduced in version 1.0, and the specification refers readers to a separate Data Generator example in its appendix. Data Generator Data Generator

The Dataset Instance metadata object provides information about the dataset instance and its content. Dataset Instance is a data generator-delivered instance of a FOCUS Dataset. For example, a Data Generator may provide multiple datasets utilizing the FOCUS specification, including multiple instances of the FOCUS Cost and Usage dataset, each representing a different time granularity. Dataset Instance is the metadata that describes each dataset instance a data generator delivers, since one generator may provide several datasets, such as multiple instances of the Cost and Usage dataset at different time granularities. DatasetInstance must be present in the metadata, must be a non-null collection of objects, and must contain at least one object for every FOCUS dataset the data generator supports; each object must not be null and must be associated with one and only one FOCUS dataset. Each object must carry three non-null string properties: DatasetInstanceId, an identifier that must be unique within the data generator and should be a GUID; DatasetInstanceName, a human-readable name provided by the data generator; and FocusDatasetId, which must match the Dataset ID of one of the FOCUS datasets defined in the specification, indicating which dataset, such as Cost and Usage or Contract, the data aligns with. All were introduced in version 1.3. Dataset Instance ID Dataset Instance Name Dataset Instance FOCUS Dataset ID

The recency metadata object and its contents provide information about how up-to-date FOCUS datasets are and when they have been updated. Recency metadata records how up to date FOCUS datasets are and when they were updated. Recency may be present in the Metadata; it must be a non-null collection of objects, each associated with exactly one DatasetInstance and retrievable without inspecting dataset instance artifacts, and it should be updated when the data generator updates the corresponding artifact. Each object must carry DatasetInstanceId, where a GUID is recommended, and DatasetInstanceLastUpdated, and RecencyLastUpdated must be present in the metadata. For datasets that are not time series, DatasetInstanceComplete must be present as a Boolean. For time series datasets, TimeSectors must be present as a collection of at least one object, each with TimeSectorStart, TimeSectorEnd later than the start, TimeSectorComplete and TimeSectorLastUpdated, updated or added whenever the data generator updates or provides artifacts. Time sectors are periods relative to ChargePeriodStart and ChargePeriodEnd; the data generator sets their length, suggested to match the report's time granularity, and defines what complete means. The schema metadata object and its content provide information about the structure of the data provided. Schema metadata describes the structure of the data a FOCUS delivery provides. Schema must be present in the Metadata as a collection of objects, with at least one object for every DatasetInstance and each object tied to exactly one. A new Schema object must be added whenever the structure of dataset instance artifacts changes, including added or removed columns, ColumnDefinition changes, or FocusVersion or DataGeneratorVersion updates; artifacts must reference the Schema object they conform to, and it must be retrievable independently of them. Each object must carry SchemaId, where a GUID is recommended, FocusVersion matching the published FOCUS version the artifacts conform to, CreationDate, DatasetInstanceId and ColumnDefinition, and may carry DataGeneratorVersion, which must change when FocusVersion changes. ColumnDefinition must hold one object per column, each with ColumnName and DataType. Conditional or recommended attributes are Deprecated, PreviousColumnName for renamed columns, ProviderTagPrefixes for the Tags column, StringEncoding, StringMaxLength, NumericPrecision and NumberScale. Schema for validating the Contract Commitment Applicability column JSON object structure in FOCUS datasets This JSON schema defines the object held in the Contract Commitment Applicability column, which states which entities a contract commitment applies to. IsGlobalScope (default false) means the commitment applies to all entities, and IsComplexScope (default false) means the applicability logic exceeds what the schema can express. They cannot both be true, and when either is true, Inclusions must be empty or omitted. Otherwise InclusionOperator ("And" or "Or") and at least one Inclusions rule are required. Optional Exclusions require an ExclusionOperator. Each rule requires a Dimension (a FOCUS column name), an Operator (In, NotIn, StartsWith, NotStartsWith, Contains, NotContains, EndsWith, Exists or DoesNotExist) and at least one string in Values. The wildcard "*" must be the only value, and Exists and DoesNotExist require it. An Applicability object, with Cost and Usage fractions from 0 to 1 (default 1) applying to ContractCommitmentCost and ContractCommitmentQuantity, can appear at top level or override it per rule. Custom properties need an x_ PascalCase prefix.

Schema for validating the Allocated Method Details column JSON object structure in FOCUS datasets This JSON schema defines the object held in the Allocated Method Details column, which describes the properties of a cost allocation. The object requires an Elements array containing at least one item. Each item requires AllocatedRatio, a number from 0 to 1 giving the percentage of overall cost derived from the corresponding method and metric. Each item may also carry UsageUnit, a string or null naming the unit measured to calculate the allocation, and UsageQuantity, a number or null giving the volume of that unit consumed. When UsageQuantity is a number, UsageUnit must be provided and must be a string; when UsageQuantity is absent or null, UsageUnit may hold anything or be absent. No other properties are allowed, except custom data generator-defined properties prefixed with x_ in PascalCase, which may appear both at the top level and within each item.

Schema for validating the Commitment Program Eligibility Details column JSON object structure in FOCUS datasets This JSON schema defines the structure of the object held in the CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails column of FOCUS datasets. The object requires one property, CommitmentPrograms, an array of at least one object identifying the commitment programs for which the usage is eligible. Each array item requires ProgramType, a string naming the specific type of commitment program available for that usage, with discount and capacity reservation given as examples of such types. No other properties are permitted, either within an array item or at the top level of the object, except custom properties defined by the data generator, whose names must begin with x_ followed by an uppercase letter in PascalCase format. An empty CommitmentPrograms array is therefore invalid under the schema.

Schema for validating the Contract Applied column JSON object structure in FOCUS datasets This JSON schema defines the structure of the object held in the ContractApplied column of FOCUS datasets. The object requires one property, Elements, an array of at least one object, each describing a contract commitment applied to the charge. Each element requires ContractId, the contract's unique identifier, and ContractCommitmentId, the identifier of the contract commitment term, both strings. It also records what was applied in one of two mutually exclusive forms: either ContractCommitmentAppliedCost holds a number and ContractCommitmentAppliedQuantity and ContractCommitmentAppliedUnit must be absent or null, or the quantity, a number, and the unit of measure, a string, both have values and the cost must be absent or null. No other properties are allowed, either within an element or at the top level, except custom data generator-defined properties whose names begin with x_ in PascalCase format.

Schema for validating the Requester Details column structure in FOCUS datasets. The column is an array of key-value entries, where each entry's value is an object of FOCUS-defined descriptive properties (Type, Name, Email) plus optional custom properties. This JSON schema defines the structure of the Requester Details column. The column is an array of key-value entries with at least one entry, and each entry requires a key and a value and allows nothing else. The key names the requester level the entry describes and must be "Principal", "Credential" or a custom key prefixed with x_ in PascalCase. The value is an object with at least one property, holding the FOCUS-defined descriptive properties Type, the kind of entity described (for example User, Service Account, API Key or Session); Name, a readable display name; and Email, an associated email address. All three are optional strings. The value may also carry custom data generator-defined properties prefixed with x_ in PascalCase, whose values may be strings, numbers, booleans, objects or arrays; no other property is allowed.

Schema for validating the SKU Price Eligibility column JSON object structure in FOCUS datasets This JSON schema validates the object held in the SKU Price Eligibility column, which sets the eligibility boundary for a price through inclusion and exclusion rules. The booleans IsGlobalScope and IsComplexScope default to false and cannot both be true: the first means eligibility is not restricted to an enumerated set of entities, the second that the logic exceeds what the schema can express. When either is true, Inclusions must be empty or omitted and InclusionOperator is not allowed; otherwise InclusionOperator (And or Or) and at least one Inclusions rule are required. Optional Exclusions holds at least one rule and requires ExclusionOperator. Each rule requires Dimension (a valid FOCUS column name), Operator (In, NotIn, StartsWith, NotStartsWith, Contains, NotContains, EndsWith, Exists or DoesNotExist) and Values (at least one string). If the wildcard "*" is used it must be the sole value, with In, Contains, Exists or DoesNotExist; Exists and DoesNotExist require it. Only custom properties named x_ plus PascalCase may be added.

items.t: Spend by provider and service category
items.b: Start here. Billed cost is what the invoice says; effective cost spreads commitment purchases across the usage they cover.
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, ServiceCategory, round(sum(BilledCost), 2) AS BilledCost, round(sum(EffectiveCost), 2) AS EffectiveCost, count(*) AS Rows FROM CostAndUsage GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY EffectiveCost DESC;

items.t: What kinds of charge are in the bill?
items.b: ChargeCategory is a closed list: Usage, Purchase, Tax, Credit, Adjustment. Look for values that should not be there.
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, ChargeCategory, ChargeClass, count(*) AS Rows, round(sum(BilledCost), 2) AS BilledCost FROM CostAndUsage GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ServiceProviderName, ChargeCategory;

items.t: Effective savings rate by provider
items.b: ESR = 1 - effective cost / list cost, on usage. Correction rows (ChargeClass = 'Correction') are excluded. The sample's costs are anonymised, so read the method, not the number.
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, round(sum(ListCost), 2) AS ListCost, round(sum(EffectiveCost), 2) AS EffectiveCost, round(1 - sum(EffectiveCost) / nullif(sum(ListCost), 0), 4) AS EffectiveSavingsRate FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND ChargeClass IS NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ListCost DESC;

items.t: Commitment discount utilisation
items.b: Used vs Unused commitment, by type. Utilisation = used effective cost / (used + unused).
items.x: SELECT CommitmentDiscountType, round(sum(EffectiveCost) FILTER (WHERE CommitmentDiscountStatus = 'Used'), 2) AS UsedCost, round(sum(EffectiveCost) FILTER (WHERE CommitmentDiscountStatus = 'Unused'), 2) AS UnusedCost, round(sum(EffectiveCost) FILTER (WHERE CommitmentDiscountStatus = 'Used') / nullif(sum(EffectiveCost), 0), 4) AS Utilisation FROM CostAndUsage WHERE CommitmentDiscountId IS NOT NULL AND ChargeCategory = 'Usage' GROUP BY ALL;

items.t: Tag keys in use (allocation hygiene)
items.b: Every tag key and how much cost carries it. Spot the near-duplicates that break allocation.
items.x: SELECT k AS TagKey, count(*) AS Rows, round(sum(EffectiveCost), 2) AS EffectiveCost FROM CostAndUsage, unnest(json_keys(Tags)) AS t(k) WHERE Tags IS NOT NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY Rows DESC;

items.t: Allocation coverage: share of cost with an application tag
items.b: The classic allocation KPI: what share of cost can be attributed to an owner?
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, round(sum(EffectiveCost), 2) AS EffectiveCost, round(sum(EffectiveCost) FILTER (WHERE Tags ->> '$.application' IS NOT NULL) / nullif(sum(EffectiveCost), 0), 4) AS ApplicationTaggedShare FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargeCategory = 'Usage' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY EffectiveCost DESC;

items.t: Daily cost trend
items.b: Cost per day by provider, from ChargePeriodStart.
items.x: SELECT date_trunc('day', ChargePeriodStart) AS Day, ServiceProviderName, round(sum(EffectiveCost), 2) AS EffectiveCost FROM CostAndUsage GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY Day, ServiceProviderName;

items.t: Top 10 resources by effective cost
items.b: Where the money goes, resource by resource.
items.x: SELECT ResourceId, ResourceName, ServiceName, round(sum(EffectiveCost), 4) AS EffectiveCost FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ResourceId IS NOT NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY EffectiveCost DESC LIMIT 10;

items.t: Marketplace purchases (service provider is not the host)
items.b: FOCUS 1.3+ separates who sells the service from who hosts it. In this sample, Red Hat and Datadog are bought through AWS.
items.x: SELECT HostProviderName, ServiceProviderName, InvoiceIssuerName, ServiceName, ChargeCategory, round(sum(BilledCost), 2) AS BilledCost, count(*) AS Rows FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ServiceProviderName <> HostProviderName GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY BilledCost DESC;

items.t: Data quality checks a validator would make
items.b: Rows that break simple FOCUS rules. Each count should be zero in conformant data.
items.x: SELECT 'ChargeCategory outside the allowed values' AS Check, count(*) AS Rows FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargeCategory NOT IN ('Usage', 'Purchase', 'Tax', 'Credit', 'Adjustment') UNION ALL SELECT 'ChargePeriodEnd not after ChargePeriodStart', count(*) FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargePeriodEnd <= ChargePeriodStart UNION ALL SELECT 'Charge period outside its billing period', count(*) FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargePeriodStart < BillingPeriodStart OR ChargePeriodEnd > BillingPeriodEnd UNION ALL SELECT 'Usage row with no ConsumedQuantity', count(*) FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND ConsumedQuantity IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT 'Tag key with leading or trailing spaces', count(*) FROM CostAndUsage, unnest(json_keys(Tags)) AS t(k) WHERE k <> trim(k);

items.t: AI token cost by model and token type (1.5 examples)
items.b: FOCUS 1.5 puts model identity and token type in SkuPriceDetails. Switch the data source to the spec 1.5 worked examples to see rows.
items.x: SELECT SkuPriceDetails ->> '$.ModelId' AS ModelId, SkuPriceDetails ->> '$.TokenDirection' AS TokenDirection, SkuPriceDetails ->> '$.TokenCacheAction' AS TokenCacheAction, sum(ConsumedQuantity) AS Tokens, round(sum(EffectiveCost), 4) AS EffectiveCost, round(sum(EffectiveCost) * 1e6 / nullif(sum(ConsumedQuantity), 0), 4) AS CostPerMillionTokens FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ConsumedUnit = 'Tokens' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ModelId, TokenDirection, TokenCacheAction;

items.t: Example SQL Query
items.x: SELECT BillingAccountId, BillingAccountName, BillingAccountType, SubAccountId, SubAccountName, SubAccountType, BillingCurrency, SUM(BilledCost) FROM CostAndUsage WHERE BillingPeriodStart >= ? AND BillingPeriodEnd < ? GROUP BY BillingAccountId, BillingAccountName, BillingAccountType, SubAccountId, SubAccountName, SubAccountType, BillingCurrency

items.t: Effective Cost Per Million Tokens
items.b: Effective cost per one million tokens, by model, SKU, token direction, and cache action. The query also returns the pricing quantity and unit, which can differ from the token count when a provider prices tokens in blocks (e.g., per one million tokens):
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.ModelDeveloper') AS ModelDeveloper, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.ModelId') AS ModelId, SkuId, SkuPriceId, SkuMeter, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.TokenDirection') AS TokenDirection, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.TokenCacheAction') AS TokenCacheAction, BillingCurrency, PricingUnit, SUM(ConsumedQuantity) AS TotalTokens, SUM(PricingQuantity) AS TotalPricingQuantity, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS TotalEffectiveCost, SUM(EffectiveCost) * 1000000 / NULLIF(SUM(ConsumedQuantity), 0) AS EffectiveCostPerMillionTokens FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargeCategory='Usage' AND ServiceCategory='AI and Machine Learning' AND ConsumedUnit='Tokens' AND ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd <= ? GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.ModelDeveloper'), JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.ModelId'), SkuId, SkuPriceId, SkuMeter, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.TokenDirection'), JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.TokenCacheAction'), BillingCurrency, PricingUnit

items.t: Token Consumption Volume Over Time
items.b: Token consumption volume over time, by service, service subcategory, model, token direction, and cache action:
items.x: SELECT ChargePeriodStart, InvoiceIssuerName, ServiceProviderName, ServiceName, ServiceSubcategory, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.ModelDeveloper') AS ModelDeveloper, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.ModelId') AS ModelId, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.TokenDirection') AS TokenDirection, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.TokenCacheAction') AS TokenCacheAction, SUM(ConsumedQuantity) AS TotalTokens FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargeCategory='Usage' AND ServiceCategory='AI and Machine Learning' AND ConsumedUnit='Tokens' AND ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd <= ? GROUP BY ChargePeriodStart, InvoiceIssuerName, ServiceProviderName, ServiceName, ServiceSubcategory, JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.ModelDeveloper'), JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.ModelId'), JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.TokenDirection'), JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceDetails, '$.TokenCacheAction')

items.t: Example SQL Query
items.x: SELECT BillingPeriodStart, BillingPeriodEnd, InvoiceId, BillingCurrency, SUM(BilledCost) FROM CostAndUsage GROUP BY BillingPeriodStart, BillingPeriodEnd, InvoiceId, BillingCurrency

items.t: Find the List Prices in Force at a Point in Time
items.b: One *SKU* can still return the same public rate more than once. A *service provider* can publish a separate usage record, with its own SKU Price ID, for consumption a *commitment discount* covers. That record also holds the list price. SKU Price Description and Commitment Discount Category are returned so these rows can be told apart.
items.x: SELECT SkuId, SkuPriceId, SkuPriceDescription, CommitmentDiscountCategory, PricingUnit, QuantityTierMinimum, QuantityTierMaximum, PricingCurrency, PricingCurrencyCategory, UnitPrice FROM SkuPrice WHERE ServiceProviderName = ? AND PricingServiceName = ? AND ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND UnitPriceType = 'List' AND (SkuPriceEffectiveStart IS NULL OR SkuPriceEffectiveStart <= ?) AND (SkuPriceEffectiveEnd IS NULL OR SkuPriceEffectiveEnd > ?) ORDER BY SkuId, UnitPrice

items.t: Estimate the Cost of a Planned Workload
items.b: The query prices each line at the public rate from the "List" record. Replacing `SP.UnitPriceType = 'List'` with `SP.ContractId = ? AND SP.UnitPriceType = 'Contracted'` prices it at the rate negotiated under a *contract* instead. A line whose SKU Price ID has no "Contracted" record under that *contract* then returns with its price columns null. The Unit Price Type filter is still needed, because one *contract* can have both a "Base" and a "Contracted" record for the same SKU Price ID.
items.x: WITH PlannedUsage (ServiceProviderName, SkuPriceId, PlannedQuantity, PlannedDate) AS ( VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?) ) SELECT PU.ServiceProviderName, PU.SkuPriceId, PU.PlannedDate, SP.SkuPriceDescription, SP.PricingUnit, SP.QuantityTierMinimum, SP.QuantityTierMaximum, PU.PlannedQuantity, SP.UnitPrice, SP.PricingCurrency, SP.PricingCurrencyCategory, PU.PlannedQuantity * SP.UnitPrice AS EstimatedPricingCurrencyCost FROM PlannedUsage PU LEFT JOIN SkuPrice SP ON SP.ServiceProviderName = PU.ServiceProviderName AND SP.SkuPriceId = PU.SkuPriceId AND SP.UnitPriceType = 'List' AND (SP.SkuPriceEffectiveStart IS NULL OR SP.SkuPriceEffectiveStart <= PU.PlannedDate) AND (SP.SkuPriceEffectiveEnd IS NULL OR SP.SkuPriceEffectiveEnd > PU.PlannedDate) ORDER BY SP.PricingCurrencyCategory, SP.PricingCurrency, EstimatedPricingCurrencyCost DESC

items.t: Identify the Prices a Billing Account is Eligible For
items.b: > **Note:** This query checks only rules whose `Dimension` key is `BillingAccountId` and whose `Operator` is `In`. That includes the `["*"]` wildcard, which matches every account. Rows flagged `IsComplexScope` are returned for review, not resolved. The query does not check `Exclusions`, so it can return a price for an account that `Exclusions` removes. Some prices have neither global nor complex scope and have `Inclusions` that do not name `BillingAccountId`. Under the implicit wildcard rule in the SKU Price Eligibility column definition, such a price places no limit on billing account, but this query does not return it. The query compares values exactly as written, while the SKU Price Eligibility column definition compares them without regard to case. A full check applies `InclusionOperator` across all inclusion rules, then removes any entity caught by `Exclusions`, in the order the SKU Price Eligibility column definition gives. Doesn't run in DuckDB as published. It tests whether a value is in a list with BigQuery's `value IN UNNEST(array)` form, which DuckDB doesn't support (DuckDB writes it list_contains(array, value)). The specification says this query may need small changes for a particular database engine.
items.x: SELECT SkuPriceId, ContractId, UnitPriceType, SkuPriceDescription, UnitPrice, PricingCurrency, SkuPriceEligibility FROM SkuPrice WHERE ServiceProviderName = ? AND (SkuPriceEffectiveStart IS NULL OR SkuPriceEffectiveStart <= ?) AND (SkuPriceEffectiveEnd IS NULL OR SkuPriceEffectiveEnd > ?) AND ( JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceEligibility, '$.IsGlobalScope') = 'true' OR JSON_VALUE(SkuPriceEligibility, '$.IsComplexScope') = 'true' OR EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM UNNEST(JSON_EXTRACT_ARRAY(SkuPriceEligibility, '$.Inclusions')) AS INC WHERE JSON_VALUE(INC, '$.Dimension') = 'BillingAccountId' AND JSON_VALUE(INC, '$.Operator') = 'In' AND ( ? IN UNNEST(JSON_VALUE_ARRAY(INC, '$.Values')) OR '*' IN UNNEST(JSON_VALUE_ARRAY(INC, '$.Values')) ) ) ) ORDER BY SkuPriceId, ContractId, UnitPriceType

items.t: Separate Usage Rates from Purchase Fees and Credit Values
items.b: This query answers what kinds of prices a catalog holds. Knowing that keeps a forecast from leaving out purchase fees or reading a credit value as a usage rate. It takes a service provider and a point in time, and it shows how the catalog splits across Charge Category. A forecast built only on "Usage" rates leaves out any purchase fees the architecture also has to pay. So each category is counted on its own, not added together. Only "List" records are counted, so the counts and price ranges describe the public catalog, not the prices of any one *contract*. Pricing Currency Category is returned so a rate priced in a *consumption currency* is not read as money.
items.x: SELECT ChargeCategory, PricingUnit, PricingCurrency, PricingCurrencyCategory, COUNT(*) AS SkuPriceCount, MIN(UnitPrice) AS LowestPublicUnitPrice, MAX(UnitPrice) AS HighestPublicUnitPrice FROM SkuPrice WHERE ServiceProviderName = ? AND UnitPriceType = 'List' AND (SkuPriceEffectiveStart IS NULL OR SkuPriceEffectiveStart <= ?) AND (SkuPriceEffectiveEnd IS NULL OR SkuPriceEffectiveEnd > ?) GROUP BY ChargeCategory, PricingUnit, PricingCurrency, PricingCurrencyCategory ORDER BY ChargeCategory, PricingUnit

items.t: Find Announced Price Changes and Scheduled Retirements
items.b: SKU Price Created and SKU Price Last Updated are returned to show when the record entered the catalog and when it last changed. The dataset shows prices as of the date it is captured. To rebuild a price history the *service provider* does not publish, a *practitioner* keeps dataset instances over time. The *practitioner* then compares them on SKU Price Effective Start and SKU Price Effective End. The two timestamps cannot replace that comparison, because a correction can update a record after its effective window has closed.
items.x: SELECT SkuId, SkuPriceId, SkuPriceDescription, UnitPrice, PricingCurrency, SkuPriceEffectiveStart, SkuPriceEffectiveEnd, SkuPriceCreated, SkuPriceLastUpdated FROM SkuPrice WHERE ServiceProviderName = ? AND UnitPriceType = 'List' AND (SkuPriceEffectiveStart > ? OR SkuPriceEffectiveEnd > ?) ORDER BY SkuPriceEffectiveStart, SkuPriceEffectiveEnd

items.t: Compare List Prices Across Regions
items.b: This query answers how the public rate for each *SKU* varies by location. A deployment decision can then weigh the price difference between regions. It takes a service provider, a pricing service name, and a point in time. Rows are sorted by SKU ID, because SKU ID stays the same across the price details a *SKU* varies by, including location. SKU Price ID may not, since a *service provider* may publish a separate SKU Price ID for each region. This query applies where the *operating model* includes regions.
items.x: SELECT SkuId, SkuPriceId, PricingRegionId, PricingUnit, QuantityTierMinimum, QuantityTierMaximum, PricingCurrency, UnitPrice FROM SkuPrice WHERE ServiceProviderName = ? AND PricingServiceName = ? AND ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND UnitPriceType = 'List' AND (SkuPriceEffectiveStart IS NULL OR SkuPriceEffectiveStart <= ?) AND (SkuPriceEffectiveEnd IS NULL OR SkuPriceEffectiveEnd > ?) ORDER BY SkuId, PricingCurrency, UnitPrice

items.t: Report on Commitment Discount Purchases
items.x: SELECT MIN(ChargePeriodStart) AS ChargePeriodStart, MAX(ChargePeriodEnd) AS ChargePeriodEnd, ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, CommitmentDiscountId, CommitmentDiscountType, CommitmentDiscountUnit, CommitmentDiscountQuantity, ChargeFrequency, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND ChargeCategory = 'Purchase' AND CommitmentDiscountId IS NOT NULL GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, CommitmentDiscountId, CommitmentDiscountType, CommitmentDiscountUnit, CommitmentDiscountQuantity, ChargeFrequency

items.t: Report on Corrections
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, ChargeCategory, ServiceCategory, ServiceName, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost FROM CostAndUsage WHERE BillingPeriodStart >= ? AND BillingPeriodEnd < ? AND ChargeClass = 'Correction' GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, ChargeCategory, ServiceCategory, ServiceName

items.t: Report Recurring Charges
items.x: SELECT BillingPeriodStart, CommitmentDiscountId, CommitmentDiscountName, CommitmentDiscountType, ChargeFrequency, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost FROM CostAndUsage WHERE BillingPeriodStart >= ? AND BillingPeriodStart < ? AND ChargeFrequency = 'Recurring' AND CommitmentDiscountId IS NOT NULL GROUP BY BillingPeriodStart, CommitmentDiscountId, CommitmentDiscountName, CommitmentDiscountType, ChargeFrequency

items.t: Report on Unused Commitment Discounts
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, CommitmentDiscountId, CommitmentDiscountType, CommitmentDiscountStatus, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS TotalEffectiveCost FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND CommitmentDiscountStatus = 'Unused' GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, CommitmentDiscountId, CommitmentDiscountType, CommitmentDiscountStatus

items.t: Report on Unused Capacity Reservations
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, CapacityReservationId, CapacityReservationStatus, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS TotalEffectiveCost FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND CapacityReservationStatus = 'Unused' GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, CapacityReservationId, CapacityReservationStatus

items.t: Identify Eligible Uncovered Spend by Program Type
items.b: > **Note:** When a *charge* is eligible for multiple *commitment program* types, it appears once per eligible type. Costs are not deduplicated across types, since each type represents an independent purchasing opportunity.
items.x: SELECT CU.ServiceProviderName, CU.ServiceName, JSON_VALUE(CP, '$.ProgramType') AS EligibleProgramType, SUM(CU.BilledCost) AS EligibleUncoveredCost FROM CostAndUsage CU CROSS JOIN UNNEST(JSON_EXTRACT_ARRAY(CU.CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails, '$.CommitmentPrograms')) AS CP WHERE CU.ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND CU.ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND CU.ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND CU.CommitmentDiscountId IS NULL AND CU.CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails IS NOT NULL -- Replace with provider-specific discount-bearing program types AND JSON_VALUE(CP, '$.ProgramType') IN ('Flexible Spend Plan', 'Resource Reservation') GROUP BY CU.ServiceProviderName, CU.ServiceName, JSON_VALUE(CP, '$.ProgramType') ORDER BY EligibleUncoveredCost DESC

items.t: Calculate Commitment Discount Coverage Rate with Eligibility-Adjusted Denominator
items.b: > **Note:** Unused *commitment discount* rows ([Commitment Discount Status](#datamodel.costandusage.commitmentdiscountstatus) is "Unused") have Commitment Discount ID populated and would artificially inflate both the numerator and the denominator, so the query excludes them. Commitment Discount Status is null on rows without a *commitment discount*, so the filter also keeps null values.
items.x: WITH CommitmentDiscountEligible AS ( SELECT CU.ServiceProviderName, CU.EffectiveCost, CU.CommitmentDiscountId FROM CostAndUsage CU WHERE CU.ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND CU.ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND CU.ChargeCategory = 'Usage' -- Exclude unused commitment rows; keep rows without a commitment discount AND (CU.CommitmentDiscountStatus IS NULL OR CU.CommitmentDiscountStatus != 'Unused') AND ( -- Include covered rows in the denominator CU.CommitmentDiscountId IS NOT NULL -- If uncovered, check if the JSON array contains an eligible program type OR EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM UNNEST(JSON_EXTRACT_ARRAY(CU.CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails, '$.CommitmentPrograms')) AS CP WHERE JSON_VALUE(CP, '$.ProgramType') IN ('Flexible Spend Plan', 'Resource Reservation') ) ) ) SELECT ServiceProviderName, SUM(CASE WHEN CommitmentDiscountId IS NOT NULL THEN EffectiveCost ELSE 0 END) AS CoveredCost, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS EligibleCost, SUM(CASE WHEN CommitmentDiscountId IS NOT NULL THEN EffectiveCost ELSE 0 END) / NULLIF(SUM(EffectiveCost), 0) AS CommitmentCoverageRate FROM CommitmentDiscountEligible GROUP BY ServiceProviderName

items.t: Compare Commitment Opportunities Across Providers (Cross-Provider with SaaS)
items.b: > **Note:** As with the first query above, when a *charge* is eligible for multiple *commitment program* types, it appears once per eligible type. Removing the `EligibleProgramType` grouping without deduplicating would inflate totals.
items.x: WITH CommitmentDiscountEligible AS ( SELECT CU.ServiceProviderName, JSON_VALUE(CP, '$.ProgramType') AS ProgramType, CU.EffectiveCost, -- EffectiveCost = BilledCost for uncovered rows; used here for ratio consistency CASE WHEN CU.CommitmentDiscountId IS NULL THEN CU.EffectiveCost ELSE 0 END AS UncoveredCost FROM CostAndUsage CU CROSS JOIN UNNEST(JSON_EXTRACT_ARRAY(CU.CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails, '$.CommitmentPrograms')) AS CP WHERE CU.ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND CU.ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND CU.ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND CU.CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails IS NOT NULL -- Replace with provider-specific discount-bearing program types AND JSON_VALUE(CP, '$.ProgramType') IN ('Flexible Spend Plan', 'Resource Reservation') ) SELECT ServiceProviderName, ProgramType AS EligibleProgramType, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS EligibleCost, SUM(UncoveredCost) AS UncoveredEligibleCost, SUM(UncoveredCost) / NULLIF(SUM(EffectiveCost), 0) AS UncoveredRate FROM CommitmentDiscountEligible GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, ProgramType ORDER BY UncoveredEligibleCost DESC

items.t: Identify Eligible Capacity Reservation Spend
items.b: > **Note:** The FOCUS specification requires Capacity Reservation ID to not be null when a *charge* represents unused capacity, but only recommends populating it when a *charge* is related to a used *capacity reservation*. Where a data generator does not populate Capacity Reservation ID on used rows, this query will show those rows with a null Capacity Reservation Status.
items.x: SELECT CU.ServiceProviderName, CU.ServiceName, JSON_VALUE(CP, '$.ProgramType') AS EligibleProgramType, CU.CapacityReservationId, CU.CapacityReservationStatus, SUM(CU.BilledCost) AS BilledCost, COUNT(*) AS RowCount FROM CostAndUsage CU CROSS JOIN UNNEST(JSON_EXTRACT_ARRAY(CU.CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails, '$.CommitmentPrograms')) AS CP WHERE CU.ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND CU.ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND CU.ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND CU.CommitmentProgramEligibilityDetails IS NOT NULL AND JSON_VALUE(CP, '$.ProgramType') IN ('Advance Resource Commitment', 'Zonal Resource Commitment') GROUP BY CU.ServiceProviderName, CU.ServiceName, JSON_VALUE(CP, '$.ProgramType'), CU.CapacityReservationId, CU.CapacityReservationStatus ORDER BY BilledCost DESC

items.t: Report on Initial Contract Commitment
items.b: This query takes inputs of a time range via [Charge Period Start](#datamodel.costandusage.chargeperiodstart) and [Charge Period End](#datamodel.costandusage.chargeperiodend), then presents the aggregation of initial *contract commitments* from the Cost and Usage dataset per [Service Provider Name](#datamodel.costandusage.serviceprovidername) and Contract Commitment ID by filtering on the specified time range, along with [Charge Category](#datamodel.costandusage.chargecategory) of "Purchase".
items.x: SELECT MIN(CU.ChargePeriodStart) AS ChargePeriodStart, MAX(CU.ChargePeriodEnd) AS ChargePeriodEnd, CU.ServiceProviderName, JSON_VALUE(CA, '$.ContractCommitmentId') AS ContractCommitmentId, SUM(CAST(JSON_VALUE(CA, '$.ContractCommitmentAppliedCost') AS FLOAT64)) AS ContractCommitmentAppliedCost FROM CostAndUsage CU CROSS JOIN UNNEST(JSON_EXTRACT_ARRAY(CU.ContractApplied, '$.Elements')) AS CA WHERE JSON_VALUE(CA, '$.ContractCommitmentAppliedCost') IS NOT NULL AND ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND ChargeCategory = 'Purchase' GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, ContractCommitmentId ORDER BY ServiceProviderName, ContractCommitmentId

items.t: Report on Usage Against Contract Commitment
items.b: This query takes inputs of a time range via Charge Period Start and Charge Period End, then presents the aggregation of the application of *contract commitments* from the Cost and Usage dataset per Service Provider Name and Contract Commitment ID by filtering on the specified time range, along with Charge Category of "Usage".
items.x: SELECT MIN(CU.ChargePeriodStart) AS ChargePeriodStart, MAX(CU.ChargePeriodEnd) AS ChargePeriodEnd, CU.ServiceProviderName, JSON_VALUE(CA, '$.ContractCommitmentId') AS ContractCommitmentId, SUM(CAST(JSON_VALUE(CA, '$.ContractCommitmentAppliedCost') AS FLOAT64)) AS ContractCommitmentAppliedCost FROM CostAndUsage CU CROSS JOIN UNNEST(JSON_EXTRACT_ARRAY(CU.ContractApplied, '$.Elements')) AS CA WHERE JSON_VALUE(CA, '$.ContractCommitmentAppliedCost') IS NOT NULL AND ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND ChargeCategory = 'Usage' GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, ContractCommitmentId ORDER BY ServiceProviderName, ContractCommitmentId

items.t: Report on Usage Against Contract Commitment by Category
items.b: This query takes inputs of a time range via Charge Period Start and Charge Period End, then presents the aggregation of the application of *contract commitments* from the Cost and Usage dataset per Service Provider Name and Contract Commitment ID by filtering on the specified time range, along with Charge Category of "Usage". It also joins in the Contract Commitment dataset to provide further information about each *contract commitment* (in this case, the contract, category, type, start and end date/time, committed cost, and committed quantity and unit). It reports applied cost only, so Contract Applied entries that record an applied quantity without an applied cost are excluded. Doesn't run in DuckDB as published. In the GROUP BY, ContractCommitmentId matches both the SELECT alias built from JSON_VALUE(CA, ...) and the CC.ContractCommitmentId column. DuckDB takes the table column, so the JSON_VALUE expression in the SELECT list is left ungrouped. (Standard SQL doesn't allow SELECT aliases in GROUP BY at all.) Whether BigQuery accepts it hasn't been checked here.
items.x: SELECT MIN(CU.ChargePeriodStart) AS ChargePeriodStart, MAX(CU.ChargePeriodEnd) AS ChargePeriodEnd, CU.ServiceProviderName, CC.ContractId, JSON_VALUE(CA, '$.ContractCommitmentId') AS ContractCommitmentId, CC.ContractCommitmentCategory, CC.ContractCommitmentType, CC.ContractCommitmentPeriodStart, CC.ContractCommitmentPeriodEnd, CC.BillingCurrency, CC.ContractCommitmentCost, CC.ContractCommitmentQuantity, CC.ContractCommitmentUnit, SUM(CAST(JSON_VALUE(CA, '$.ContractCommitmentAppliedCost') AS FLOAT64)) AS ContractCommitmentAppliedCost FROM CostAndUsage CU CROSS JOIN UNNEST(JSON_EXTRACT_ARRAY(CU.ContractApplied, '$.Elements')) AS CA INNER JOIN ContractCommitment CC ON JSON_VALUE(CA, '$.ContractCommitmentId') = CC.ContractCommitmentId WHERE JSON_VALUE(CA, '$.ContractCommitmentAppliedCost') IS NOT NULL AND ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND ChargeCategory = 'Usage' GROUP BY CU.ServiceProviderName, CC.ContractId, ContractCommitmentId, CC.ContractCommitmentCategory, CC.ContractCommitmentType, CC.ContractCommitmentPeriodStart, CC.ContractCommitmentPeriodEnd, CC.BillingCurrency, CC.ContractCommitmentCost, CC.ContractCommitmentQuantity, CC.ContractCommitmentUnit ORDER BY CU.ServiceProviderName, CC.ContractCommitmentCategory, ContractCommitmentId

items.x: SELECT Tags, ConsumedUnit, SUM(BilledCost), SUM(EffectiveCost), SUM(ConsumedQuantity) FROM CostAndUsage WHERE BillingPeriodStart >= ? AND BillingPeriodEnd < ? GROUP BY Tags, ConsumedUnit

items.t: Discount Effectiveness by Service
items.x: WITH AggregatedData AS ( SELECT ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, BillingAccountName, BillingCurrency, ServiceName, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS TotalEffectiveCost, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost, SUM(CASE WHEN ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND BilledCost = 0 AND EffectiveCost != 0 THEN 0 ELSE ContractedCost END) AS TotalContractedCost, SUM(CASE WHEN ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND BilledCost = 0 AND EffectiveCost != 0 THEN 0 ELSE ListCost END) AS TotalListCost FROM CostAndUsage WHERE BillingPeriodStart >= ? AND BillingPeriodEnd < ? AND ChargeClass IS NULL GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, BillingAccountName, BillingCurrency, ServiceName ) SELECT ServiceProviderName, BillingAccountId, BillingAccountName, BillingCurrency, ServiceName, TotalEffectiveCost, TotalBilledCost, TotalListCost, (1 - TotalContractedCost / NULLIF(TotalListCost, 0)) * 100 AS ContractedDiscount, (1 - TotalEffectiveCost / NULLIF(TotalListCost, 0)) * 100 AS EffectiveDiscount FROM AggregatedData

items.t: Cash vs. Accrual Comparison by Billing Period
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, InvoiceIssuerName, BillingPeriodStart, BillingPeriodEnd, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS TotalEffectiveCost, SUM(EffectiveCost) - SUM(BilledCost) AS CostBasisDifference FROM CostAndUsage WHERE BillingPeriodStart >= ? AND BillingPeriodEnd < ? GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, InvoiceIssuerName, BillingPeriodStart, BillingPeriodEnd HAVING ABS(SUM(EffectiveCost) - SUM(BilledCost)) > 0.01

items.t: Commitment Discount Savings for a Charge Period Range
items.b: For each *commitment discount* within a [*charge period*](#glossary:chargeperiod) range, compares the Contracted Cost of the usage it covered with its total Effective Cost, including the unused portion (i.e., where [Commitment Discount Status](#datamodel.costandusage.commitmentdiscountstatus) is "Unused"). The difference is the net savings attributable to the *commitment discount*, and a negative value means the unused portion cost more than the *commitment discount* saved on covered usage.
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, BillingCurrency, CommitmentDiscountId, MIN(ChargePeriodStart) AS ChargePeriodStart, MAX(ChargePeriodEnd) AS ChargePeriodEnd, SUM(CASE WHEN CommitmentDiscountStatus = 'Used' THEN ContractedCost ELSE 0 END) AS TotalContractedCost, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS TotalEffectiveCost, SUM(CASE WHEN CommitmentDiscountStatus = 'Used' THEN ContractedCost ELSE 0 END) - SUM(EffectiveCost) AS CommitmentDiscountSavings FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND CommitmentDiscountId IS NOT NULL GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, BillingCurrency, CommitmentDiscountId

items.t: Billing Period vs. Charge Period Comparison
items.b: A *billing period* identifies when a *charge* is invoiced, while a *charge period* identifies when the *charge* was incurred, so filtering the same data by each can return different totals. This query separates the *charges* in each *billing period* into those whose *charge period* falls within the *billing period* and those whose *charge period* extends outside it (e.g., purchases that cover a longer term).
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, BillingCurrency, BillingPeriodStart, BillingPeriodEnd, CASE WHEN ChargePeriodStart >= BillingPeriodStart AND ChargePeriodEnd <= BillingPeriodEnd THEN 'Within Billing Period' ELSE 'Outside Billing Period' END AS ChargePeriodAlignment, MIN(ChargePeriodStart) AS EarliestChargePeriodStart, MAX(ChargePeriodEnd) AS LatestChargePeriodEnd, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS TotalEffectiveCost FROM CostAndUsage WHERE BillingPeriodStart >= ? AND BillingPeriodEnd < ? GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, BillingCurrency, BillingPeriodStart, BillingPeriodEnd, CASE WHEN ChargePeriodStart >= BillingPeriodStart AND ChargePeriodEnd <= BillingPeriodEnd THEN 'Within Billing Period' ELSE 'Outside Billing Period' END

items.t: Extract JSON from Allocated Method Details

AND BillingPeriodEnd < ? GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, BillingPeriodStart, BillingPeriodEnd, ServiceCategory, ServiceName, RegionId, RegionName, PricingUnit

items.t: Commitment Discount Effective Cost Breakdown
items.b: Analyzes *commitment discount* [*amortization*](#glossary:amortization) by *charge period*, capturing costs based on when *resources* were consumed.
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, CommitmentDiscountId, CommitmentDiscountStatus, ChargePeriodStart, ChargePeriodEnd, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS TotalEffectiveCost FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND CommitmentDiscountId IS NOT NULL AND ChargeCategory = 'Usage' GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, CommitmentDiscountId, CommitmentDiscountStatus, ChargePeriodStart, ChargePeriodEnd

items.t: Effective Cost by Consumed Quantity and Pricing Quantity
items.b: Compares the quantity consumed with the quantity priced for the same usage *charges*, per SKU. [Consumed Quantity](#datamodel.costandusage.consumedquantity) and [Consumed Unit](#datamodel.costandusage.consumedunit) measure what was used (e.g., hours, GB), while [Pricing Quantity](#datamodel.costandusage.pricingquantity) and [Pricing Unit](#datamodel.costandusage.pricingunit) measure what the unit price was applied to, which can use a different unit or block size (e.g., GB-months, blocks of 1,000 requests). Dividing Effective Cost by each quantity gives the cost per unit consumed and the effective price per unit priced. Rows where Consumed Quantity is null (e.g., when [Charge Category](#datamodel.costandusage.chargecategory) is not "Usage", or when Commitment Discount Status is "Unused") are excluded.
items.x: SELECT ServiceProviderName, BillingCurrency, ServiceName, SkuId, ConsumedUnit, PricingUnit, SUM(ConsumedQuantity) AS TotalConsumedQuantity, SUM(PricingQuantity) AS TotalPricingQuantity, SUM(EffectiveCost) AS TotalEffectiveCost, SUM(EffectiveCost) / NULLIF(SUM(ConsumedQuantity), 0) AS EffectiveCostPerConsumedUnit, SUM(EffectiveCost) / NULLIF(SUM(PricingQuantity), 0) AS EffectiveCostPerPricingUnit FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargePeriodStart >= ? AND ChargePeriodEnd < ? AND ChargeCategory = 'Usage' AND ConsumedQuantity IS NOT NULL GROUP BY ServiceProviderName, BillingCurrency, ServiceName, SkuId, ConsumedUnit, PricingUnit

items.t: Reconcile Cost and Usage to Invoice Detail by Invoice ID
items.b: This query validates that the sum of costs for all service usage in the Cost and Usage dataset equals the total non-tax *charges* in the Invoice Detail dataset for a specific *invoice*.
items.x: SELECT COALESCE(ID.InvoiceId, CU.InvoiceId) AS InvoiceId, ID.TotalBilledCost_InvoiceDetail, CU.TotalBilledCost_CostAndUsage, (COALESCE(ID.TotalBilledCost_InvoiceDetail, 0) - COALESCE(CU.TotalBilledCost_CostAndUsage, 0)) AS Variance FROM ( SELECT InvoiceId, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost_InvoiceDetail FROM InvoiceDetail WHERE ChargeCategory != 'Tax' GROUP BY InvoiceId ) ID FULL OUTER JOIN ( SELECT InvoiceId, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost_CostAndUsage FROM CostAndUsage WHERE ChargeCategory != 'Tax' GROUP BY InvoiceId ) CU ON ID.InvoiceId = CU.InvoiceId WHERE COALESCE(ID.InvoiceId, CU.InvoiceId) = ?

items.t: Reconcile Cost and Usage to Invoice Detail by Invoice Detail ID
items.b: This query compares each non-tax record in the Invoice Detail dataset for a specific *invoice* with the sum of the *charges* in the Cost and Usage dataset that reference it, identifying the *invoice* line items where the two datasets differ.
items.x: SELECT ID.InvoiceIssuerName, ID.InvoiceId, ID.InvoiceDetailId, ID.InvoiceIssueStatus, ID.BillingCurrency, ID.BilledCost AS BilledCost_InvoiceDetail, CU.TotalBilledCost_CostAndUsage, (ID.BilledCost - COALESCE(CU.TotalBilledCost_CostAndUsage, 0)) AS Variance FROM InvoiceDetail ID LEFT JOIN ( SELECT InvoiceIssuerName, InvoiceId, InvoiceDetailId, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilledCost_CostAndUsage FROM CostAndUsage GROUP BY InvoiceIssuerName, InvoiceId, InvoiceDetailId ) CU ON ID.InvoiceIssuerName = CU.InvoiceIssuerName AND ID.InvoiceId = CU.InvoiceId AND ID.InvoiceDetailId = CU.InvoiceDetailId WHERE ID.InvoiceIssuerName = ? AND ID.InvoiceId = ? AND ID.ChargeCategory != 'Tax' ORDER BY ID.InvoiceDetailId

items.t: Reconcile Multi-Currency Settlement Using Lineage IDs
items.b: This query demonstrates how to use Payment Currency Invoice Detail ID to reconcile granular records (denominated in the billing currency) against the aggregate records used for payment (denominated in the payment currency). This resolves the "Divergent Grain" problem.
items.x: SELECT PaymentCurrencyInvoiceDetailId, BillingCurrency, PaymentCurrency, SUM(BilledCost) AS TotalBilled_BillingCurrency, SUM(PaymentCurrencyBilledCost) AS TotalBilled_PaymentCurrency, -- Calculate effective exchange rate for the group SUM(PaymentCurrencyBilledCost) / NULLIF(SUM(BilledCost), 0) AS EffectiveExchangeRate FROM InvoiceDetail WHERE InvoiceId = ? GROUP BY PaymentCurrencyInvoiceDetailId, BillingCurrency, PaymentCurrency ORDER BY PaymentCurrencyInvoiceDetailId

items.t: Validate Tax Variance
items.b: This query identifies the tax component present in the Invoice Detail dataset that is typically excluded from the Cost and Usage dataset, allowing for a complete three-way match between usage, tax, and the total *invoice* amount.
items.x: SELECT InvoiceId, SUM(CASE WHEN ChargeCategory = 'Tax' THEN BilledCost ELSE 0 END) AS TotalTaxAmount, SUM(CASE WHEN ChargeCategory != 'Tax' THEN BilledCost ELSE 0 END) AS TotalServiceAmount, SUM(BilledCost) AS GrandTotalPayable FROM InvoiceDetail WHERE InvoiceId = ? GROUP BY InvoiceId
